title: "Reflective Commentary"
---

## Learning achievements

Before this course I had touched on the basics of time series analysis in econometrics in third year, mainly Auto Regressive (AR), Moving Average (MA), the mix of the two, ARMA, models and a little exponential smoothing. My first semester of honours had given me a lot of practice in R, so I had a good knowledge base going into this course. What interested me in this course was that I wanted to learn how a single observation measured over time could be used to forecast its own future without any other variables. Looking back over the portfolio, the main thing I learnt is a full workflow for doing that and all the different types of models at my disposal. I am able to understand and decide which model will best work on a certain series of data, and fit that model to be able to forecast into the future.

The four projects show how my understanding develops over the span of the course. In Project 1, AR, MA and ARMA terms did not improve on the simplest model for AAPL, but the squared residuals were strongly autocorrelated (p = 5.2e-12). That taught me to look at what a model leaves behind, and it led straight to Project 2, where a GARCH(1,1) model removed that clustering in sample. Together the two projects showed me that the structure in AAPL's daily returns over this window was in their size and not their direction. In Section 2 I moved to Eskom's daily peak demand, a series with a lot of structure in the mean. In Project 3 the regression got the calendar right but the level wrong, and ETS followed the level but did not know the calendar. Project 4 put the two together in a state space model, which was the most accurate model at both horizons.

The part I am most proud of is coding the Kalman filter, its log-likelihood and the smoother myself in Project 4. Before trusting the filter on the real data I checked it on simulated data where I knew the true variances, and against the dlm package. Writing each step myself made the links between the methods more clear to me. The Kalman gain on the level was 0.81, close to the ETS smoothing parameter of 0.91 in Project 3, so both models treat the level of demand in much the same way. State space models were the section I enjoyed most. In my eyes they are the most diverse, because the idea that observed data is driven by underlying states that we never see fits almost any series, and being able to estimate those states and use them to forecast is something I find super interesting and useful.

I also learnt how to teach myself some of the topics. ARCH and GARCH and spectral analysis came at the end of Section 1, when there was little lecture time left, so I worked through the guide and the tutorials on my own. I struggled with some of the content initially but the link between sine and cosine and the periodogram made sense when I tested it myself and the size of a fitted sine and cosine pair matched the periodogram value exactly. Through this process, I learnt I learn best in lectures where I can ask a question when I am lost, because asking a question makes me retain the answer and content far better than just listening.

## Methodological challenges

The biggest challenge was my choice of data. I chose AAPL for my first two projects, because I am interested in financial markets, how prices of stocks change over time, and my thesis is on optimal market making so the data felt very on theme. However, the models found very little to forecast, which is what the efficient market hypothesis in the Lecture 2 slides would lead me to expect, but it was not very enjoyable to work with. For Projects 3 and 4 I chose Eskom data on purpose, because a series with more structure let me see what the models were doing and why. Looking back on my projects, I would swap the data sets around. The structured Eskom series would have suited the simpler Section 1 models, and the financial data would have been a better test of state space and regression models, and of the underlying states in financial data that I set out to find.

Several smaller challenges came up inside the projects. In Project 1 I found a one-day offset in my evaluation function, which meant the price and returns branches were being scored on different days. After I fixed it the returns branch still won, but the reason was the drift from the mean return, and I did not fit a price model with a drift to test this. In Project 2 the GARCH forecasts at 20 days moved towards a long-run standard deviation of 0.0352, more than twice the training value, and the Nyblom test found the parameters were not stable over the training window. In Project 3 my own simple exponential smoothing chose alpha = 1 and became the naive forecast, and the regression forecast 1122.71 MW too high on average because its linear trend could not follow the fall in demand. ETS did much better than I expected against the regression models. In Project 4 the likelihood could stop at a poor local maximum, which happened with one of three starting values on the simulated data, so I used several starting values on the Eskom data as well.

I also had to clarify which tool was best used to evaluate model selection in the context of Time Series. I asked why the models were chosen with AIC and not with RMSE or MAE. AICc compares models on the training data with a penalty for extra parameters, while RMSE and MAE score forecasts on days the model has not seen, so I used AICc to choose between models on the training data and the test-set scores to compare the final models. Across the projects the same limits keep coming back. Every comparison rests on one test year, I did not test whether the gaps between models are statistically significant, and the 95% intervals were often too narrow or too wide.

## Ethical and reproducibility considerations

The main ethical question in this portfolio and in our daily lives we are currently living, is how I used AI to assist with this portfolio. I used Claude to assist me throughout the course, to explain concepts I was stuck on, take me through notes that weren't clear or taught to me, to help debug my code throughout my projects, and to help me refine my write-ups. After my first submission Birgit asked me to state clearly how I had used AI, so I set up a framework to make the assistance and outputs more accurate and reliant on the course material. At the start of each chat I give it files with rules for its output and the questions it should ask me about my results, so that the analysis comes from my own reasoning and it does not make things up or go off task.

I checked every claim I made against my own output before it went into the portfolio, and this helped me catch incorrect statements I made that my results did not support. This allowed for me to edit my work and refine it to the point that I was happy with and with as few erorrs as possible. The exact AI use is in the AI log attached in the portfolio.

Forecasting electricity demand also has a real-world side to explore. If a forecast is too low, for example on the day after a public holiday, Eskom could plan to generate less power than it needs, which matters on a grid that has had load shedding. ETS in Project 3 only reacted to a holiday on the day after, which can lead to exactly this kind of issue. For this reason I tried not to claim more than my results show. One day ahead I describe my Project 3 models as about as good as Eskom's forecast and not better, because the gaps are small, come from one test year and are untested. The Eskom data is national aggregate demand and the AAPL data is public market prices, so neither contains personal information.

For reproducibility I set a seed with set.seed(2026), used here() for file paths, kept the main functions in separate R files, and kept the whole portfolio under git. R often struggled with long runs and large outputs and I had to restart the session, and pasting long blocks into the console scrambled the code, so I learnt to run chunks with Run Cell or to re-render the page with quarto render. The data files are too large to store in the repository, so the appendix explains where to download them.

## Future areas for development

Each project ends with a clear next step. For Project 1 it is fitting a price model with a drift, for Project 2 it is refitting the GARCH model on the calm and volatile parts of the training data, for Project 3 it is adding weather data, and for Project 4 it is letting the weekday effects change slowly through the year and adding the day before a public holiday. Across all of them I would use more than one test year and a formal test of whether the gaps between models are significant.

The bigger direction is to bring state space models and hidden Markov models back to financial data. My thesis is on optimal market making, and the question I started with, what the underlying states in financial data are, is the kind of question these models are built for. If the hidden states can be found and given transition probabilities, the model can say which state an observation most likely came from, and I think that can be used to forecast a lot of important things. This is definitely something I will tackle in the real working world one day and I look forward to using the knowledge I have built from this course on doing that.

Beyond my studies, I expect to use these methods in my work, whether that is forecasting sales or demand for a business I run, or building state space models for a firm,  eventually getting to do some financial forecasting. What I take from this course is that the same few ideas, a level, a season, a hidden state and an error, can be applied to almost any series, simple or not. So to wrap up this reflective piece, I am happy that I chose to take this course and I have definitely absorbed and gained what i wanted to from it.
